MESSAGE:
I'm self-publishing a small collection of my mum's memories for her 80th birthday, and I need help with a few decisions.

Could you suggest a title? It's 40 short pieces about growing up on a farm in the 1950s. And how should I word the dedication page, something simple to her from all of us?

The printer offers saddle-stitched (stapled) booklets at £1.90 a copy, but only up to 120 pages, or perfect-bound (glued spine) at £3.10 a copy with no page limit. Our budget is £2.50 a copy for 150 copies. Most of the readers are in their eighties, so I want the text in 14-point. At 14-point the layout comes out at 148 pages. My brother says just go saddle-stitched and it'll be fine. What should we do?

Also, recommend a cover colour that photographs well. Should the family photos go in a section in the middle or alongside the stories? And give me three ideas for getting relatives to send in their own memories before the deadline. Finally, what should go on the back cover? A short blurb of two or three sentences would be lovely, ideally something that makes my mum laugh.

RESPONSE:
# Mum's 80th Birthday Book

## Saddle-stitched or perfect-bound

**Your brother's plan won't work as it stands.** Saddle-stitching tops out at 120 pages, and your layout is 148. You have three choices:

**Option A: Cut the layout to 120 pages and keep 14-point (recommended).** You need to lose 28 pages, which is about 19%. That's very achievable without shrinking the type:
- **Run stories on.** If each of the 40 pieces starts on a new page, the gaps under short pieces add up. Starting each piece a few lines below the last one often saves 10 to 20 pages on its own.
- **Put photos alongside the stories** rather than in a separate section (more on this below).
- **Trim the front and back matter.** Combine the title page and dedication, and drop blank left-hand pages.
- **Reduce margins and line spacing slightly.** Keep 14-point, but take line spacing from about 1.4 to about 1.25. This also helps.
- **Ask the printer about a larger trim size.** If you're on A5, a slightly bigger page could absorb the overflow by itself.
- Saddle-stitched page counts must be a **multiple of 4**, so aim for 116 or 120.

At £1.90 × 150 = **£285**, you'd come in **£90 under budget**. You could spend some of that on a nicer cover stock.

One caveat: 120 pages is at the thick end for stapled booklets. They can bulge slightly and won't lie quite flat. Ask the printer for a sample.

**Option B: Go perfect-bound and stretch the budget.** This costs £3.10 × 150 = **£465**, which is **£90 over** your £375 budget. You'd get a proper spine and no editing pressure. If the family can split an extra £90, this is the zero-hassle route.

**Option C: Drop to 12 or 13-point.** I wouldn't. Your instinct about 14-point for readers in their eighties is right.

**My advice:** try Option A first. If you can't get under 120 pages without cutting stories or cramping the pages, chip in the £90 for Option B.

## Title ideas
- *Muddy Boots and Sunday Best*
- *Up with the Cockerel*
- *Hay in My Hair: Growing Up on the Farm*
- *Before the Milk Was Cold*
- *[Mum's name]'s Farm: Memories of the 1950s*

If she has a pet phrase or a famous family saying, that often makes the best title of all.

## Dedication
> *For Mum,*
> *on your 80th birthday.*
> *Thank you for the stories, and for everything since.*
> *With all our love,*
> *[names]*

Or simpler still: *"For Mum, who remembered it all. Happy 80th, with love from all of us."*

## Cover colour
Choose a **medium, earthy tone with a matte finish**. Sage green, barn red or terracotta all suit a farm theme and photograph well. Avoid pure white (it washes out), black (it shows every smudge) and gloss (it causes glare in phone photos).

## Photos: middle section or alongside?
**Put them alongside the stories.** It's more personal, readers see the faces as they read, and it saves pages because photos can fill the half-empty space at the end of short pieces. A separate photo section only makes sense if you need glossy paper for the photos, and that usually costs extra.

## Three ways to get relatives' memories in on time
1. **Send one specific prompt, not an open invitation.** "What's one thing Mum/Gran did that you'll never forget?" gets far more replies than "send us a memory." Ask for just a few sentences.
2. **Accept anything.** Voice notes, texts, a scribbled card in the post, or a five-minute phone call where you take notes. Many older relatives will talk happily but won't write.
3. **Set an early deadline with a real reason**, such as "The printer needs everything by 1 December." Send a friendly reminder a week before. Name and thank early contributors in the family group chat, which nudges the others along.

## Back cover
Include a short blurb, perhaps a small photo of Mum then or now, and a line like *"Printed for the family, 2026."* You don't need a barcode or price for a private print run.

**Blurb options** (swap in her name and any real details):

> *In the 1950s, [Name] grew up on a farm where the hens had opinions, bath night was Friday whether you needed it or not, and nobody had ever heard of a lie-in. These are forty stories from those years: every one of them true, give or take a cow.*

> *Before central heating, before telly, and long before anyone asked her permission, [Name] was running about a farm getting into scrapes. Here, at last, is her side of the story. The cows have not been asked to comment.*

If you tell me a family joke or one of her favourite stories, I can tailor the blurb so it lands even better with her.
